title: Prediction: Nvidia Stock Is Going to Soar After Nov. 17 - The Motley Fool
content: With hyperscalers' capital expenditures holding up, Nvidia has a lot working in its favor. Nvidia (NVDA -4.22%) has been one of the stock market's biggest winners over the last several years. Its market cap now tops $5 trillion, and the stock is still on the rise -- it's up nearly 15% in 2026 so far. Investors who bought the stock three years ago are sitting on a whopping 429% return. Stretch that timeline to five years, and Nvidia is up 759%. Those are outstanding returns, but I don't think Nvidia is finished rewarding shareholders. In fact, I believe it could have another big move coming after the chipmaker reports its fiscal 2027 third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17. Here's why I'm bullish on Nvidia stock heading into its next earnings report. It's difficult to appreciate just how quickly Nvidia is growing until you look at the numbers. The company generated $96.2 billion in revenue during its fiscal 2027 second quarter, which ended July 26. That was a 106% increase from the prior-year period, with data center revenue climbing 117% to $89 billion. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. And Nvidia is making an enormous amount of money on those sales. Its non-GAAP gross margin reached 75%, meaning Nvidia retained 75 cents of every revenue dollar after accounting for the direct costs of producing its products. Adjusted earnings per share increased 120% to $2.22. Those aren't the financial results of a company whose best days are necessarily behind it. For the fiscal third quarter, Nvidia is forecasting revenue of approximately $108 billion, representing another substantial increase from the $57 billion it generated a year earlier. Wall Street expects even more. According to Yahoo! Finance, analysts are projecting revenue of approximately $109 billion and adjusted earnings of $2.47 per share. That would amount to revenue growth of roughly 91% and earnings growth of 90% from the year-ago quarter. Nvidia has already demonstrated that it can deliver extraordinary growth even at its now enormous scale. Another strong quarter, particularly if management raises its outlook, could give investors another reason to push the stock higher. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been bullish about the company's future, and his confidence isn't limited to its potential to sell more graphics processing units (GPUs). Huang believes global spending on AI infrastructure could reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030. He has also indicated that Nvidia expects to sell twice as many chips in 2027 as it does in 2026. Earnings from big tech companies give Nvidia investors a lot to look forward to. Meta Platforms raised the low end of its 2026 capital spending range from $135 billion to $145 billion, Alphabet held its $195 billion to $205 billion capex budget range steady, and Microsoft trimmed its 2026 plan slightly from $175 billion to $170 billion. However, Alphabet also said it expects spending to rise significantly in 2027, and Microsoft's CFO said she expects spending to accelerate in the first half of 2027 on higher component costs and delayed deliveries. Amazon, which reported its latest results after the closing bell on Oct. 29, also reaffirmed its plan to spend $220 billion this year. As a group, hyperscalers are expected to spend more than $1 trillion on capex next year, and since these companies are among Nvidia's biggest customers, budgets that hold steady or rise support its demand picture heading into its report after the close on Nov. 17. But there's another part of Nvidia's growth story that I find particularly compelling. The company's next-generation Vera Rubin architecture is designed to deliver more computing power from each gigawatt of electricity it consumes. And Nvidia expects the platform to generate considerably more revenue for each gigawatt of computing capacity. Huang explained during the company's August earnings call that Nvidia's revenue opportunity increased from approximately $18 billion per gigawatt with its Grace Hopper platform to $25 billion with the Grace Blackwell platform that succeeded it in late 2024. With the new Vera Rubin platform, that figure could reach $40 billion. That's a 60% increase from Blackwell, without requiring its data center customers to add more electrical capacity. If customers continue buying Nvidia's increasingly sophisticated AI systems, the company has an opportunity to grow revenue at a faster rate than it grows its chip shipments. Despite its incredible stock performance, Nvidia trades at approximately 23 times forward earnings. That's a premium to the S&P 500's forward price-to-earnings ratio of 18.6, but I believe it's extremely reasonable given Nvidia's growth. Remember, analysts expect Nvidia's earnings to grow by approximately 95% during fiscal 2027. They're also forecasting another 71% increase in fiscal 2028. With Wall Street already expecting nearly $109 billion in quarterly revenue, Nvidia has a high bar to clear. Moreover, even an earnings beat doesn't guarantee a stock rally if investors are disappointed by management's guidance. But I'm not particularly worried about Nvidia's premium valuation. We're talking about a company that's more than doubling quarterly revenue, maintaining gross margins around 75%, and preparing to sell increasingly valuable AI computing systems. Paying 23 times forward earnings for that kind of performance doesn't strike me as excessive. But with AI infrastructure spending continuing, Nvidia's earnings growing rapidly, and its valuation looking reasonable relative to its prospects, I believe the odds favor another strong performance from Nvidia in its next earnings report. That's why I'm bullish on Nvidia heading into Nov. 17 -- and why I think shares could climb substantially afterward. title: History Says Now Is the Perfect Time to Buy Nvidia Stock - AOL.com
content: Nvidia trades only at a slight premium to the broader market. 2026 hasn't been the best year for Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA). While it's up 13% versus 11% from the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC), Nvidia investors don't expect market-beating performance; they expect market-crushing performance. When you look at Nvidia's results, it's easy to see it should be doing better, as it grew revenue at 106% in the second quarter (Q2). Over the long term, company growth and stock performance tend to be highly correlated, so what's up with the disconnect? I believe it's just the market lagging behind, and history tells us that right now is an incredible buying opportunity. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » The best way to value Nvidia from a current and historical perspective is to utilize the forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio. This metric uses analysts' estimates for the full fiscal year to price the stock, so it bakes in some growth. At the start of a fiscal year, these measures tend to look pretty cheap, as there is a full year's worth of growth ahead. When you get halfway through the fiscal year (Q3 results aren't available yet), this starts to become a more conservative estimate, as only six months of growth are projected. So, sometimes stocks start to look a tad expensive toward the end of the year. In both 2024 and 2025, Nvidia's stock reached 40 times forward earnings before the year was over. That's not the case this year. At just under 23 times forward earnings, Nvidia hasn't seen the end-of-year rally it normally does. This raises the question of why, and I think it's simply because the market is trying to call Nvidia's bluff (even if it's wrong). The S&P 500 trades at about 19.2 times forward earnings, so Nvidia trades at only a slight premium to the broader market. This is essentially the market conveying that after this year, it expects market-average growth from Nvidia. But according to Nvidia and Wall Street analysts, that's a gross error. Nvidia itself told investors during its Q2 earnings call that it expects 70% revenue growth next year. It's rare for a company to provide next-year guidance six months before the year begins, but it shows the confidence Nvidia has in its future growth. This is likely because many of its clients have locked in orders for next year, giving it high visibility of what's to come. Wall Street analysts are also bullish, expecting 68% revenue growth next fiscal year. All of this adds up to a company that will deliver excellent growth next year, which should result in huge returns. If we value Nvidia's stock using next fiscal year's estimates, the stock trades for just 13.3 times earnings. So, if Nvidia hits all projections and the stock doubles, that means it would only trade for 26 times trailing earnings. That's a reasonable price tag for a company of Nvidia's stature and pedigree, so expecting the stock to rise significantly over the next year isn't out of the question. As a result, I think the historical record is pretty clear that the future is bright for Nvidia. But that's just 2027. Beyond 2027, there's a broad expectation for the AI build-out to last through at least 2030, giving Nvidia even more time to capitalize on a generational growth opportunity. There are few better buys in the market than Nvidia right now, and investors shouldn't wait around too long; now is the time to strike. content: U.S. stock indices ended higher on Wednesday as the Federal Reserve’s decision to keep interest rates unchanged helped cool some inflation worries, while weak earnings from Alphabet led the Nasdaq 100 to drop after-hours. The S&P 500 ended Wednesday 0.3% higher, the Nasdaq 100 rose 0.5%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.2%. The Russell 2000, which tracks small-cap stocks, added 0.4%. Meanwhile, Nasdaq-100 futures lost 1.2%. S&P 500 futures declined 0.5%, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures lost 17 points, or 0.03% at the time of writing. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) gained 0.6%, and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) rose 0.2%. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) ended 0.5% higher on Wednesday. Meanwhile, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and the iShares Semiconductor ETF jumped about 2% each on Wednesday as gains in AMD, Micron Tech (MU) and Broadcom (AVGO). The broader Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT) rose 0.6%. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits for SPY improved to ‘neutral’ from ‘bearish’, while it remained in ‘bearish’ territory for DIA and QQQ. The Federal Reserve opted to keep its target interest rate steady on Wednesday, but financial markets focused on Chair Kevin Warsh's announcement of a structural shift in the frequency of future interest rate decisions. The central bank held interest rates steady at 3.75% to 4% amid elevated inflation and a strong job market. The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 10–2 vote. Under Warsh’s revamped framework, the FOMC will issue rate decisions at seven of its eight scheduled sessions in 2027, reserving one meeting exclusively for broad monetary policy strategy without issuing a formal rate statement. By 2028, the central bank plans to reduce its rate-setting votes to six per year, leaving two gatherings devoted entirely to strategic evaluations. “The Fed appears comfortable being patient for now as financial conditions have evolved broadly in line with expectations,” Luis Alvarado at Wells Fargo Investment Institute told Bloomberg. “But patience should not be confused with complacency.” Meanwhile, Alphabet Inc. (GOOG, GOOGL) shares slid about 11% after-hours after it reported third-quarter financial results that highlighted strong top-line revenue growth across its core digital ad and cloud operations, though massive investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure and investment losses squeezed profitability. These corporate reports arrive as Wall Street sharpens its focus on the artificial intelligence ecosystem. Shares of Lumentum Holdings Inc (LITE) soared 10% after hours on Wednesday following a report that Marvell Technology is in talks to buy it in a potential megadeal. A deal between Marvell and the data center optics maker could be announced as soon as next week, Bloomberg reported, citing unnamed people familiar with the matter. A final deal hasn’t been reached, and details could change, the report said. After Wednesday’s market close, Lumentum has a market value of about $83 billion, while Marvell is valued near $221 billion. Shares of MRVL tumbled 8% following the report. Marvell is a fabless semiconductor designer focused on data-infrastructure solutions, while Lumentum makes optical and photonic products such as lasers, optical components, and networking systems used in cloud and AI data centers. Lumentum’s indium-phosphide technology is particularly in high demand; CEO Michael Hurlston has previously said that the company is essentially sold out of certain products into 2029 and is under-shipping demand by substantial margins due to the fast-paced nature of AI data center buildouts. Marvell, too, is strengthening its position in  the AI space, recently inking a partnership with Google on custom chips. The company also completed acquiring Celestial AI, specialized in photonic interconnect technology to remove data bottlenecks in AI data centers, earlier this year. A potential combination would give Marvell access to scarce, high-performance optical components which can help ease bottlenecks in AI clusters by replacing copper interconnects which are more limited in capacity. (MSFT) share price inched 3% higher after-hours on Wednesday after the software maker’s first-quarter results surpassed Wall Street expectations, propelled by surging demand for its artificial intelligence tools and cloud computing platform. For the three months ended Sept. 30, the technology giant reported total revenue of $92.3 billion, representing a 19% increase compared to the same period last year. Adjusted diluted earnings per share reached $4.89, outpacing average analyst projections of $4.72. "We are delivering greater capability, choice, control, and cost efficiency for customers across our entire stack," said Satya Nadella, chairman and chief executive officer of Microsoft. "By helping organizations build and own their own intelligence, and earning trust through agent safety and security, we are translating our innovation into growing adoption and real-world impact across every industry." The core driver of the quarter’s growth was the company's cloud operations. Total Microsoft Cloud revenue hit $63.9 billion, an increase of 30% year-over-year. Sales at Azure, Microsoft’s flagship cloud computing division, jumped 48%, surpassing Wall Street estimates of 44% growth. Commercial remaining performance obligation—a key measure of future contracted revenue—soared 73% to $677 billion, signaling sustained enterprise commitment to Microsoft's ecosystem. In the Agents and Infrastructure segment, total revenue rose 25% to $76.8 billion. Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue saw an 18% increase on an adjusted basis, while consumer cloud sales grew 17%. "We delivered a strong start to the fiscal year," said Amy Hood, executive vice president and chief financial officer. "Results exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income, and earnings per share." To keep pace with computing demands for AI workloads, Microsoft expanded its capital expenditures by 30% to $45.2 billion for the quarter. The heavy spending comes as major tech companies face increased investor scrutiny over data center outlays, though analysts noted Microsoft's execution remains disciplined relative to market expectations. However, even amid rising capex, the firm’s free cash flow remained net positive, helping calm some markets that the AI buildout spend might not generate required revenue and in turn weigh on financials. Meanwhile, performance in consumer-facing divisions was mixed. The Devices and Consumer segment recorded $15.5 billion in revenue, down 3% from the prior-year period. While search and advertising revenue (excluding traffic acquisition costs) gained 12%, Windows OEM and devices revenue dropped 22%, and Xbox content and services revenue slipped 2%. Microsoft expects Q2 revenue to come in between $96 and $97.1 billion, higher than the $95.6 billion analysts polled by Fiscal.ai expect. The company also expects its capex to soar to $50 billion in Q2, while expecting its cash flow to remain net positive for the whole of FY27. Shares of Nvidia Corp (NVDA) slipped 1% on Wednesday  following reports that the U.S. Department of Justice has inquired about how its planned acquisition of Hugging Face could affect competition in artificial intelligence. According to a report from Reuters, citing people familiar with the matter, department officials have asked whether the Hugging Face deal would allow Nvidia to control a key distribution point for AI models and tools. The questioning adds to the years-long probe by antitrust regulators on Nvidia’s conduct, which kicked off under former President Joe Biden, the report said. The probe is reportedly continuing with no indication that current President Donald Trump has any involvement. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has a relationship with Trump and recently joined the President on his diplomatic trip to China. The DOJ’s recent line of questioning covers the company’s acquisitions, investments, sales practices, and whether it has pressured customers, sources told Reuters. As part of the probe, the DOJ has reportedly examined Nvidia’s other acquisition deals, including the December 2025 deal to buy SchedMD, sources told Reuters. The department has also scrutinized Nvidia's conduct following other transactions, including its licensing deal with chip startup Groq and its acquisition of Run.ai, the report added. Nvidia announced in early September that it had agreed to buy Hugging Face for approximately $12.93 billion. The transaction includes roughly $11.9 billion payable to Hugging Face’s investors and an equity-based retention program of up to about $1 billion for employees who join Nvidia. Hugging Face operates a widely used platform that hosts millions of open-source AI models, datasets, and applications, serving millions of developers and hundreds of thousands of companies. It is often described as a central hub for open AI development. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pledged that the platform will remain open to models, frameworks, clouds, and computing platforms from across the industry, and that Nvidia’s own chips will not be required to use it. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027. ORCL stock has been under pressure so far this year amid mounting concerns that ballooning debt loads and high interest rates would make the tech titan's heavy AI investments unsustainable. Chief Financial Officer Hilary Maxson announced that Oracle expects to achieve $30 billion in free cash flow by the fiscal year ending in May 2029 at its investor day in Las Vegas. The forecast heavily outperformed Wall Street expectations, as data compiled by Bloomberg and FactSet indicated that analysts anticipated the metric to remain deeply negative during that period. Fueling the optimism is a robust revenue trajectory. Oracle reaffirmed its target of $225 billion in total revenue by fiscal 2030, signaling an average annual growth rate of roughly 35%. Operating margins are projected to climb past 40% by the end of the decade. To manage the heavy capital expenditures required for the build-out, Oracle outlined a disciplined funding strategy, which included a pledge to limit total additional funding needs between fiscal 2027 and 2030 to $20 billion, split evenly between equity and debt. The company is executing a massive data center build-out to support major clients like OpenAI, stepping into direct competition with established hyperscalers like Amazon (AMZN) and Google (GOOGL). Maxson noted that Oracle plans to deliver an additional seven gigawatts of data center capacity over the next couple of years, pushing its total fleet capacity beyond 10 gigawatts by the conclusion of fiscal 2028. To put the scale in perspective, a single gigawatt of electricity generates enough power for about 750,000 U.S. homes at once. While Oracle hit negative $23.7 billion cash flow in the fiscal year ending May 2026 due to infrastructure costs, executives emphasized that capital expenditures will peak through the current and upcoming fiscal years before declining significantly in fiscal 2029. Shares of Hims & Hers (HIMS) jumped 5% on Wednesday after the Department of Health and Human Services said it would temporarily allow compounding pharmacies to produce six popular peptides. HHS said it will not go after state-licensed pharmacies, federal facilities, or licensed doctors for compounding six peptides—BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, and TB-500—as long as they follow basic rules on ingredient quality, manufacturing, safety reporting, labeling, and prescriptions written for individual patients. “...based on the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) meeting and data regarding utilization of peptides, HHS believes that there is significant interest in the use of these peptides in compounding,” HHS said, referring to the advisory committee recommendation in July that some peptides be considered for compounding. The new policy is temporary while the FDA completes formal rulemaking on the official list of bulk substances that can be used in compounding. Compounders must report serious adverse events with the use of the drugs or any product quality issues such as contamination to the FDA, HHS added.  Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. Hims has already prepared for a potential approval of peptide compounding by securing a California peptide facility and testing ingredients, while signaling interest in offering items such as sermorelin, glutathione, and NAD+ depending on final regulatory outcomes. Peptides used for recovery, inflammation, sleep, and related wellness goals have drawn strong consumer interest online, even without formal FDA approval. “We have spent years building the infrastructure we need in our very own US-based peptide manufacturing facility, developing dosing protocols with clinical experts, and setting up frameworks to better understand these emerging treatments,” the company’s Chief Medical Officer Anant Vinjamoori said after the HHS directive in a post on X. HIMS CEO Andrew Dudum also termed it “encouraging progress.” HIMS, however, has also faced setbacks this year, including an FTC lawsuit filed in late July alleging deceptive privacy practices involving data sharing with advertising platforms and misleading billing or cancellation practices. The company transitioned from offering compounded GLP-1s to branded versions earlier this year, pressuring margins despite subscriber growth. One of the liveliest ongoing debates on Wall Street is whether artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending will continue to grow at a good clip over the medium term. If it doesn't, some industry leaders will see revenue and earnings growth slow, and their share prices could sink. But if it does, some AI-focused companies still have plenty of room to run. Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), recently made comments that support the bullish outlook. Of course, Huang is hardly an unbiased observer. Still, it's worth paying attention to what he said and the potential implications for Nvidia and other AI leaders. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » First, a little bit of background on neocloud companies. Unlike traditional cloud computing providers like Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) that offer a broad range of services, neoclouds specialize in renting out the compute power needed to develop and run AI models. Neoclouds became more prominent as the AI revolution took off, but there is more room for them to grow, at least if we believe the words of Jensen Huang. In a recent interview, the CEO of Nvidia said: If you look at the fundamentals, the demand for the neoclouds is off the charts. Their capabilities are extraordinary, and so what is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth, to fund that growth. There is a lot to unpack here. First, the great news. Demand for neocloud services being off the charts is a bullish sign for Nvidia. These neoclouds purchase GPUs (graphics processing units) from the company and rent out GPU compute to other corporations. Growing demand could force these companies to expand their capacity. That means they may keep buying Nvidia's GPUs. But can they afford this massive AI build-out? That's the not-so-great news. As Huang pointed out, these companies may lack the capital necessary to purchase the infrastructure -- including GPUs -- to meet demand for their services. Recent developments support Huang's view. Companies like CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) and even Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) have said that there is more demand for their services than they can (or are willing to) provide, at least in the short term. Meanwhile, CoreWeave has raised more than $30 billion in debt and equity capital this year. Note that the company is worth about $33 billion as of writing, so it has raised capital equivalent to almost 91% of its market cap in a single year. That points to the financial bottleneck Huang mentioned and to how some neocloud companies are looking to solve it. But what does all this mean for Nvidia's prospects? One bullish scenario could go like this. CoreWeave and its neocloud peers will conjure up various ways to fund their massive AI build-outs. Perhaps they will borrow more, or resort to dilutive forms of financing (or both). Another possibility is that more competitors will enter the market upon seeing the massive, lucrative opportunity. The result: neocloud companies will continue to purchase the infrastructure necessary to meet demand for their services, and some of that money will flow directly into Nvidia's pockets. Of course, this also assumes that the AI boom will continue unabated at least over the next few years. If it doesn't, neoclouds could significantly reduce spending, leading to lower demand for Nvidia's products. Which scenario is more likely? Probably something closer to the first one. Soaring demand for neocloud services, the growing popularity of AI agents, and several other indicators support this. Medium-term projections for AI infrastructure spending remain high for these (and other) reasons. And Nvidia could be one of the biggest winners. So, it's not too late to invest in the stock, even after its amazing run in recent years. content: From Apple to Eli Lilly and Co, what are the AI-driven hedging strategies? As concerns on Wall Street about the hefty returns on tech giants' massive investments in artificial intelligence (AI) continue to mount,$Apple (AAPL.US)$Surpass on Friday$NVIDIA (NVDA.US)$, once again becoming the world's most valuable publicly traded company. Amid widespread sell-offs in tech stocks, Apple has emerged as a more defensive choice for investors, thanks to its relatively restrained capital expenditures and robust cash flow. On Friday, Apple's stock fell 1.2%, closing with a market capitalization of about $5.03 trillion; NVIDIA's shares dropped 4.2%, bringing its market cap down to $4.93 trillion. This marks the first time Apple has reclaimed the top spot on the global market-cap leaderboard since briefly surpassing NVIDIA at the end of July this year. Behind Apple's regaining the top spot in market capitalization lies a shift in the market's attitude toward the AI investment prospects of tech giants. Recently,$Intel (INTC.US)$ 、$Amazon (AMZN.US)$、 $Alphabet-A (GOOGL.US)$and$Meta Platforms (META.US)$As major tech companies have successively released disappointing financial results or earnings guidance, investors have grown concerned about the growth prospects of the tech sector and the returns on AI investments. Notably, as major tech companies continue to pour substantial capital into building AI data centers and other computing infrastructure, the market is beginning to question whether these investments can generate sufficient revenue and profits within a reasonable timeframe. Some tech giants' capital expenditures have already exceeded their operating cash flows, resulting in negative free cash flow. Both Alphabet and Amazon are experiencing this situation and are increasingly relying on the bond market to finance their investments. Meanwhile, rising interest rates are further driving up companies' financing costs. In contrast, Apple has not made large-scale investments in AI infrastructure like other tech giants, instead maintaining a relatively restrained capital expenditure strategy. This has won it favor from investors as the market re-evaluates the risks of AI investments. Data shows that Apple's stock has risen 27% year-to-date, making it not only the best-performing stock among the U.S. "Big Seven," but also outpacing NVIDIA, which ranks second, by more than double. Meanwhile, Apple's cash flow performance has also significantly surpassed that of some of its tech peers. The market expects Apple's free cash flow to grow 38% year over year in fiscal year 2026, which ends on September 30, reaching $142 billion. Strong cash flow means that Apple can support its business growth and shareholder returns without resorting to large-scale borrowing, unlike some of its competitors. Against the backdrop of rising interest rates and increasing financing costs for tech companies, this advantage is attracting growing attention from investors. As Apple regained the top spot in global market capitalization, the U.S. tech sector is undergoing a noticeable correction. Following a sharp plunge on Friday, the stock has posted a cumulative drop of over 45% in October, marking the largest monthly decline in more than four decades of data compiled by Bloomberg. Overall, Apple has once again surpassed NVIDIA, reflecting a shift in how investors evaluate large tech companies. Previously, the market favored firms that aggressively invested in AI infrastructure and could capitalize on the AI boom; now, as capital expenditures continue to rise and financing costs increase, investors are placing greater emphasis on corporate cash flow, profitability, and financial stability. If that were to happen, it could be the catalyst that starts the dominoes falling, and the AI trade could all unravel -- or so the popular narrative goes. The news highlights NVIDIA's push to move from selling chips to supplying full AI factory blueprints, from liquid-cooled Vera Rubin clusters down to on-device RTX Spark systems, tightening its role in how customers design, deploy and govern large scale AI infrastructure. The biggest risk right now is not demand; it is concentration and competition. Large cloud customers are pushing in house accelerators, and regulators are scrutinizing deals like Hugging Face. The latest Oracle expansion strengthens NVIDIA's role in third party AI infrastructure and therefore supports the core thesis rather than changing it. Scaling OCI superclusters with Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs, plus Spectrum X networking, ties directly into the idea that revenue per gigawatt rises as customers adopt full stack Vera Rubin platforms instead of buying stand alone GPUs. Operationally, the Oracle deal matters because it lets customers scale CPU and GPU capacity independently. This aligns well with agentic workloads that are relatively GPU light but CPU hungry between model calls. That supports the key catalyst that AI factories need both accelerators and Vera CPUs at scale, while leaving intact the risk that over time, hyperscalers could still shift part of that stack to their own silicon. That mix of rapid sales expansion and lower profitability per dollar of revenue sketches a future where scale matters more than peak margin, which fits the AI factory framing of Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell clusters serving enormous workloads for hyperscalers, neoclouds and industrial customers.
